items.q: Mitchell Exercise 6.1: after a first positive cancer test gives P(cancer|+) ≈ 0.21, a **second independent** positive test is run. To update, the correct Bayesian move is to:
options: use the first posterior (0.21) as the new prior and apply Bayes again
items.explain: Bayesian updating is sequential: yesterday's posterior becomes today's prior. With two independent positives the posterior for cancer rises well above 0.5. (Mitchell, Exercise 6.1.)

items.q: Mitchell Exercise 6.2 asks you to justify normalizing $P(+|cancer)P(cancer)$ and $P(+|¬cancer)P(¬cancer)$ so they sum to 1. This is valid because:
options: by the theorem of total probability the denominator $P(+)$ equals their sum
items.explain: $P(+) = P(+|cancer)P(cancer)+P(+|¬cancer)P(¬cancer)$ (total probability), so dividing each term by their sum gives the true posteriors. (Mitchell, Exercise 6.2.)

items.q: Mitchell Exercise 6.3 concerns Find-G (outputs a maximally *general* consistent hypothesis). Under a uniform prior and consistency likelihood, Find-G is guaranteed to output:
options: a MAP hypothesis (every consistent hypothesis is equally probable)
the single ML but never MAP hypothesis
items.explain: With a uniform prior and 0/1 consistency likelihood, all consistent hypotheses share the maximum posterior, so any version-space member — including Find-G's output — is a MAP hypothesis. (Mitchell, Exercise 6.3.)

items.q: Mitchell §6.4 proves that under zero-mean Gaussian noise, the maximum-likelihood hypothesis is the one that minimizes:
options: the sum of absolute errors $\sum|d_i - h(x_i)|$
the sum of squared errors $\sum (d_i - h(x_i))^2$
items.explain: Taking $\log$ of the Gaussian product likelihood and dropping $h$-independent constants leaves $-\sum(d_i-h(x_i))^2$ to maximize, i.e. minimize SSE. (Mitchell §6.4.)

items.q: Mitchell §6.6 (Minimum Description Length) interprets the MAP hypothesis as minimizing:
options: the description length: bits to encode the hypothesis + bits to encode the data given the hypothesis
items.explain: Taking $-\log_2$ of $P(D|h)P(h)$ turns MAP into minimizing $L(h)+L(D|h)$ — encode the hypothesis, then the data given it. (Mitchell §6.6, Exercise 6.5.)

items.q: Mitchell Exercise 6.6 notes the Naïve Bayes classifier corresponds to a Bayesian belief network in which:
options: every feature node is a parent of the class node
the class node is the single parent of every feature node (features independent given class)
items.explain: Naïve Bayes' conditional-independence structure is exactly a belief net with the class as the lone parent of each attribute. (Mitchell, Exercise 6.6.)

items.q: Mitchell §6.7: the Bayes optimal classifier is described as optimal because:
options: no other method using the same hypothesis space and prior can achieve lower expected error
items.explain: Averaging predictions over the full posterior yields the minimum possible expected error for the given H and priors — though it is computationally infeasible. (Mitchell §6.7.)

items.q: The EM algorithm (Dempster, Laird & Rubin 1977; Mitchell §6.12) is guaranteed to:
options: monotonically increase (never decrease) the likelihood each iteration, converging to a local optimum
items.explain: Each EM iteration provably does not decrease the data likelihood, so it converges — but only to a local maximum, hence multiple restarts. (Mitchell §6.12.)

items.q: Alpaydin Exercise 13.4: any second- (or higher-) order Markov model can be:
options: converted into an equivalent first-order model by defining new states from tuples of original states
items.explain: Define states as pairs (or k-tuples) of original states; the higher-order dependence becomes a first-order dependence among the new states. (Alpaydin, Exercise 13.4.)

items.q: Alpaydin Exercises 13.1–13.2: given an *observable* Markov model, estimating π and A from generated sequences is done by:
options: counting — start-state frequencies for π and transition frequencies for A
items.explain: For a fully observable chain, ML estimates are simple counts: $\pi_i$ from how often sequences start in $i$, $a_{ij}$ from observed $i\to j$ transitions. (Alpaydin, Exercises 13.1–13.2.)

items.q: Alpaydin calls Problem 1 (computing P(O|λ)) the **Evaluation Problem**, solved efficiently by:
items.explain: The forward procedure computes P(O|λ) in $O(N^2T)$, avoiding the $O(N^T)$ enumeration of all state paths. (Alpaydin §13.4.)

items.q: Alpaydin §13.5: the Viterbi algorithm (the Decoding Problem) and the forward procedure share the same complexity because they differ only by:
options: replacing the summation with a maximization (plus back-pointers)
items.explain: Both are $O(N^2T)$ dynamic programs; Viterbi takes the max over predecessors (and stores back-pointers) where forward takes the sum. (Alpaydin §13.5.)

items.q: Alpaydin Exercise 13.6: as you increase the number of hidden states N (training on the same data), the **training** likelihood tends to rise, but you should pick N by:
options: comparing the likelihood on a separate validation set (to avoid overfitting)
minimizing the number of states to 1
items.explain: More states fit the training data better but can overfit; choose N by validation likelihood (or domain knowledge). (Alpaydin, Exercise 13.6.)

items.q: Alpaydin §13.6: Baum-Welch is the application to HMMs of which general principle?
options: the EM algorithm (expected counts in the E-step, re-estimation in the M-step)
items.explain: Baum-Welch = EM for HMMs: the forward-backward variables give expected state/transition counts (E-step), which re-estimate π, A, B (M-step). (Alpaydin §13.6.)
